turns.en: Yeah, it probably is. And my dad is very forgiving, but I think it also ties back to why we're doing this, which I don't think everyone is thinking about until later. The way I interact with people at work—one of the things I think about, and I've talked about this at the company, is: if you can't forgive a coworker for some infraction, or something random they said to you, or some small competitive thing going on, how are we going to actually forgive people in the world? How are we going to make this work? This is a microcosm. Everything that happens as a problem in your personal life probably happens at work too. It's just that at work we can give feedback, and the stakes might be lower in some ways. That's why we cover therapy and coaching—we give coaching to people who aren't leaders, because often it's the individual contributors who go through these things. Sometimes people go through crazy emotional cycles because I made some random comment in passing, or someone said something to them, and then it really gets in their head. How much time are we wasting on that versus doing productive work? So on the one hand, you could say, 'We're a company trying to maximize shareholder value, dominate the world, and make as much money as possible.' But you're probably wasting a ton of money by not dealing with people's emotions around very silly things. And also by perpetuating—this is a pet theory of mine—very few people get to this stage of a company. When you're in it, you're trying to stay exactly on the line of success. You don't want to try too many crazy things. You want to focus on your product and what's unique about you. So you get wisdom from other people who've done it. It's kind of like what we call 'couch wisdom.' It's not really studied. It's just that this person did something before, so they give advice, and you follow it—and you get the exact same problems they had. So sometimes we try different things. People tell me, 'Hey, you should hire fast, fire fast.' Well, that has a specific set of problems.
turns.zh: 嗯，可能确实是这样。我父亲很宽容，但我觉得这又回到了我们为什么要做这件事的问题上——我不确定每个人都会在后来想到这一点。我在工作中与人互动的方式——我一直在想的一件事，我也在公司里讲过：如果你不能原谅同事的某种过失、或他们随口说的一句话、或你们之间那种小小的竞争，那我们在这个世界上到底要怎么真正原谅别人？我们怎么让它运转起来？这就是一个缩影。你个人生活中遇到的每一个问题，工作里很可能也在发生。只不过在工作中我们可以给你反馈，而且在某些方面风险可能更低。所以我们才会提供心理治疗和教练辅导——我们给非管理岗的人也配教练，因为往往就是那些个人贡献者在经历这些事。有时候，人们会因为我在旁边随口说了句话，或有人对他们说了点什么，就走入一种疯狂的情绪循环，然后就一直在脑子里转。我们到底花了多少时间来耗这些，而不是做有意义的工作？所以你可以说：‘嘿，我们是一家要最大化股东价值、要称霸世界、要赚尽可能多钱的公司。’但如果你不去处理人们因为鸡毛蒜皮的事产生的情绪，你很可能是在浪费一大笔钱。而且还在延续——这是我很私人的一个理论——很少有人能走到公司的这个阶段。当你在其中时，你拼命想踩在成功的那条线上，不想去尝试太多疯狂的事。你要专注于产品和你的独特之处。所以你从那些做成过的人那里得到些经验。这有点像我们说的‘沙发智慧’。它不是严肃研究出来的。就是这个人事先做过，于是他们给你建议，你照着做，结果遇到和他们一模一样的问题。所以有时候我们会尝试不同的方法。有人跟我说：‘你应该快招快炒。’那样做会带来一系列特定问题。

turns.en: Hire slow, fire fast.
turns.zh: 慢招快炒。

turns.en: Yeah, hire slow, fire fast.
turns.zh: 对，慢招快炒。

turns.en: You don't believe in that.
turns.zh: 你并不信这一套。

turns.en: I—
You obviously don't. You just said the fire part.
turns.zh: 你显然不信。你刚才自己都说了‘炒’的部分。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I also think there are a lot of moments where we should make decisions faster on that, but I just don't believe in these rules of thumb. At some point you shut down internally. You stop thinking about the situation. You're just following the rule.
turns.zh: 对，对。我也觉得有很多时候我们应该更快做决定，但我就是不相信这些经验法则。因为在某个时刻你会从内心封闭起来，不再去思考实际的情况，只是照着规则走。

turns.en: What other CEO-isms do you think are stupid?
turns.zh: 你觉得还有哪些 CEO 的通病很蠢？

turns.en: A lot.
turns.zh: 很多。

turns.en: Like?
turns.zh: 比如说？

turns.en: I think driving people really hard without paying attention—let me give you an example. People come in and say, 'AI is going to create a ton of productivity. We should lay off 20% of the team,' without knowing what you're actually doing. That's what makes individual contributors think execs are dumb, right? Because they go to meetings, they hear that some other person did this, and they just go and do it. There's a huge lack of empathy for the team. And I feel it sometimes too. It's like management—you know, the principal-agent problem—management versus workers, where you think, 'Why aren't people thinking correctly? Why aren't they taking action? Why aren't they owning this?' Well, the incentives aren't aligned for that.
turns.zh: 我觉得拼命压榨员工而不去关心——我举个例子。有人过来说：‘AI 会带来巨大的生产力，我们应该裁掉 20% 的人，’却根本不知道你到底在做什么。这就是为什么普通员工会觉得高管很蠢，对吧？因为他们一起去开会，听说别人这么干了，你就直接照做。而且对团队极度缺乏同理心。我自己有时候也能感觉到这一点。这就像管理中的‘委托-代理问题’——管理层和员工之间——你会想：‘为什么这些人不好好思考？为什么他们不采取行动？为什么他们不承担责任？’其实是因为激励机制没有对齐。

turns.en: Anyway, I also think—when I think about work, this is a big one for me. My definition of fun is very broad. Type two fun is fun for me. Climbing something is fun. But I think motivating people through just greed, fear, or discipline is not always optimal. You need the whole toolkit. Another word for discipline could be—
turns.zh: 总之，我还想——说到工作，这对我来说是个大问题。我对‘有趣’的定义很宽泛。‘第二类乐趣’对我来说也是乐趣，攀岩是乐趣。但我觉得只靠贪婪、恐惧或纪律来激励人，不一定是最优的。你需要整套工具。‘纪律’也可以换个词——

turns.en: The fear and greed thing. Those are the—
turns.zh: 恐惧和贪婪这套。那些就是——

turns.en: Those are all levers, by the way. Yes.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，这些都是杠杆。对。

turns.en: How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 你怎么看这件事？

turns.en: I believe in the full spectrum of things. Devotion is as good as discipline. You can't just use some of these tools without understanding that you need to both motivate your team to win and create a place you actually want to be in.
turns.zh: 我相信事物的完整光谱。投入和纪律一样重要。你不能只用其中一些工具，而不理解你需要既激励团队去赢，也创造一个你真正愿意待的地方。

turns.en: So my point is that there's something about business—this is again one of my own—that feels like you're trying to take this thing and hand it to someone else. It's like a musical chairs thing. The best businesses—I said this at the beginning—like Apple, it's like, who's actually doing all the stuff? It's Foxconn. Here's this beautiful business with all the numbers going right, but that's because I can squeeze my suppliers in this way. And I don't have to think about that supplier. It's kind of like throwing your rubbish somewhere else and saying, 'That's in China, or that's over there.' But I'm thinking, 'Hey, we live in the world together. What happens if I win but you lose?' I guess you can just jump off, and maybe you won't get caught, and no one will worry about it. But I don't want to do that, because I don't want to live with myself in this way.
turns.zh: 所以我的观点是，商业中有一种东西——这又是我自己的一个想法——让人觉得你只是想把球传到下一个人手里。就像抢椅子游戏。最好的生意——我在最开始也说过——比如苹果，问题是谁在真正做所有的事情？是富士康。这个漂亮的生意，所有数字都很好看，但那是因为我可以这样挤压供应商。然后我就不用想那个供应商了。这有点像把垃圾扔到别处，然后说：‘那是在中国，或者在那里。’但我现在想的是：‘嘿，我们一起活在这个世界上。如果我赢了但你输了，会怎么样？’我想，你也许可以直接跳下去，也许不会被抓住，也没人会为你担心。但我不想那样做，因为我不想用这种方式跟自己相处。

turns.en: Okay. I had Jack Dorsey on a few weeks ago. He's an original thinker, not central casting for CEOs. He's laid off a big chunk of his employees, but I think he's really retooled the way the company works. He's put AI at the center, delegating a lot of decisions to the center, with the people on the outside. He's rethought his org chart, its compensation—he's sort of reimagining it. I assume you're following some of that. What's your take?
turns.zh: 好。几周前我采访了杰克·多西。他是个原创的思想者，不是那种典型 CEO。他裁掉了很大一部分员工，但我觉得他真的改造了公司的运作方式。他把 AI 放在中心，把许多决策下放给中心，而人都在外围。他重新思考了组织架构、薪酬方式——他相当于在重新想象这一切。我猜你在关注这件事。你怎么看？

turns.en: I think it's hard with public companies too, because you have to ask: what's the narrative versus what's reality? I do think sometimes you do need to retool the company. Maybe you hired too many people, or things are changing. And in general, we don't have really good ways to speak the truth without—again, this is the principal-agent problem. Whatever you say is parsed: 'Is that what you really said, or does it mean something else? Are you covering something up?'
turns.zh: 我觉得上市公司也有难处，因为你得问：叙事是什么，现实又是什么？我确实认为有时候你需要改造公司。也许你招了太多人，或者事情在变化。而且总体上，我们没有特别好的方式去说真话，而不会——这又回到了委托-代理问题。你说什么都会被解读：你真是这么说的，还是别有他意？你是不是在掩盖什么？

turns.en: I don't think he was covering it up.
turns.zh: 我不觉得他在掩盖什么。

turns.en: Yeah. So that's what I mean. I think you could take it at face value and say, 'This is actually what—'
turns.zh: 对。所以这就是我的意思。我觉得你可以按表面意思来理解，然后说：‘这其实就是——’

turns.en: I think he's actually doing the thing.
turns.zh: 我觉得他确实是在做这件事。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

transcript.sec: Is he on the right track?

turns.en: And I think that's probably right.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得那大概是对的。

turns.en: And do you think he's on the right track?
turns.zh: 那你觉得他走在正确的轨道上吗？

turns.en: Um... he's got two layers. Like, he's a crazy guy. He's got a big team working on trying to make all his systems legible—get everything into that legible system. His people are really responsible for making that system as legible as it can be, then building agents on top of it, and just turning over a lot more of the decision-making over time to what he calls 'the intelligence.'
turns.zh: 嗯……他有好几层。像是个很疯狂的人。他有一个大团队在努力让他的所有系统变得可读——把所有东西都纳入那个可读的系统中。他的团队成员确实负责让那个系统尽可能可读，然后在上面构建智能体，并且随着时间推移把更多决策权交给那个他称之为“智能”的东西。

turns.en: Yeah, it's a really hard thing for me to comment on just because I haven't actually thought about it deeply enough.
turns.zh: 是啊，这对我来说真的很难评价，因为我还没有深入思考过这个问题。

turns.en: Yeah. Okay. I got a couple more just bringing you back to the philosopher king. You've got a line: 'There's no elephant in the room. The elephant is in your mind.' I can't believe he told you that. How does that apply to being a CEO?
turns.zh: 好，接下来还有几个问题，把你拉回到哲人王这个话题。你有一句话：“房间里没有大象，大象在你心里。”我简直不敢相信他对你说了那句话。那么这怎么应用到做 CEO 上呢？

turns.en: That was an off-the-cuff comment. But if I remember correctly, I have, you know, like a Q&A every week. It used to be every week, now it's every other week, and it's optional, and people show up and we talk about anything. I think my leadership style or communication style in general is to call the thing out that you might be wondering and assume that you are a smart person, and not kind of dance around it. So typically what we do in these meetings is just be like, here are all the things that you might be worried about. Well, every week actually in our all hands, I talk to people on the team constantly, and I hear various things from them about what's happening in the company, how's the culture changing or not changing, and I try to bring these things up so that we can all be aware of them. You know, so one of the things—calling them out—yeah, calling them out, like 'Hey, people feel like we're stepping on each other's toes,' and I'm like 'Okay, let's discuss that. How does that manifest? What do we want? What behavior do we want?'
turns.zh: 那是我一时脱口而出的话。但如果我没记错的话，我每周都会做一次问答。以前是每周一次，现在是隔周一次，而且是自愿参加，大家来聊任何话题。我觉得我的领导风格或者沟通风格，总体来说就是把你可能在想的事情直接说出来，并且假设你是个聪明人，而不是绕弯子。所以我们通常在这些会上做的就是，把你们可能担心的事全部摆出来。其实每周在我们的全员会上，我会不断和团队里的人聊天，听他们讲公司里发生的事、文化在怎么变化或没变化，然后我努力把这些事提出来，这样我们都能意识到。所以有一件事就是——把它们说出来——对，把它们说出来，比如“嘿，大家觉得我们好像在互相踩脚趾”，我就会说“好，那我们讨论一下。这具体是怎么体现的？我们想要什么？我们想要什么样的行为？”

turns.en: So you're calling the elephant in the room out. What about the elephant in the room?
turns.zh: 所以你是在直接点破房间里的大象。那房间里的大象呢？

turns.en: Right. So a lot of the times nothing is happening and it's just your anticipation of the problem. Or sometimes we call this like you're bringing baggage from another company where something happened to you and then you're like 'Hey, I don't trust you guys yet.' And so you're creating the problem because you're seeing this thing in your head that isn't even happening in reality. So I'm just like, 'Tell us what's actually going on so that you don't work based on some perceived reality that isn't even real.'
turns.zh: 没错。很多时候其实什么都没发生，只是你对问题的预期。或者有时候我们管这叫：你从另一家公司带来的包袱，你在那里经历过一些事，然后你就觉得“嘿，我还不信任你们。”于是你反而制造了问题，因为你看到的是你脑海里的东西，而现实里根本没有发生。所以我会说：“告诉我们到底发生了什么，这样你就不会基于一个根本不真实的、你所感知的现实来工作。”

turns.en: What do you want to do when you're old and gray like me? What's next for you?
turns.zh: 等你像我一样老了、头发白了，你想做什么？你接下来想做什么？

turns.en: It's hard to think about the future. But I happen to be an electrical engineer by training, and I have also been playing more music recently. So I want to be doing a lot of generative ambient music. I've been doing a bunch of stuff like that already. Okay. I don't know. There's something around like creating soundscapes and getting into that place where—you know, you can't really—I mean, music is all about predicting the next sound. But I've really been enjoying this idea that if you can't predict it and it's still good, then you're expanding your sound vocabulary.
turns.zh: 很难说未来会怎样。但我恰好接受过电气工程师的训练，而且最近我也在更多地玩音乐。所以我想做很多生成式氛围音乐。我已经在做一些类似的事了。好吧，我也不太确定。就是关于创造音景、进入那种境界——你知道，你不能真的……我的意思是，音乐就是要预测下一个声音。但我真的很喜欢这个想法：如果你无法预测它，但它仍然好听，那你就是在拓展你的声音词汇。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

transcript.secZh: 未来计划：生成式氛围音乐

turns.en: I appreciate you coming on. It was a wonderful conversation. Congrats on all your success.
turns.zh: 感谢你来做客。这是一次很棒的对话。祝贺你取得的所有成功。

turns.en: Thank you. Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢，谢谢。

turns.en: Hey everybody, I hope you like that episode with Kareem. I really enjoyed the conversation. I have a lot of takeaways. I'm going to give you my three and I'm going to give you a couple stories of my own that tie in. Uh, two nights ago I had dinner with Kareem and David Solomon from Goldman Sachs and TK, the CEO of Kshi. And my takeaway from the dinner was, 'Holy crap, are these three homo sapiens different and holy crap is their CEO playbook different.' And it reminds me of an old quote, you know, I think it goes, 'Be yourself. Everyone else is taken.' I think it was Oscar Wilde who said it. I leave that with you. I hope you can be yourself because everyone else is taken. There's a lot of ways to do this. I'm trying to look for the one way. The truth is there's a lot of ways to be successful as a CEO. Um, the second thing—he's sort of a philosopher—and he reminded me of something I've been working on. And people say, folks who live in the past tend to be depressed, and folks who live in the future tend to be anxious, and folks who live in today tend to be a little bit happier. I myself tend to live in the future and I'm kind of anxious. And I remember when my anxiety peaked—and this may be happening to you, so I relay it. I remember doing a company meeting around 100-150 employees and just looking out and seeing, oh my gosh, there's so many people relying on me to make really good decisions. They're taking care of their kids. They're paying their mortgages. They're taking care of their parents in a lot of cases. It wasn't actually in the tough times at the beginning. It was when we were actually scaling and starting to do pretty well that my anxiety increased. Anyway, if that's you, this is just a reminder. Living in the present is a good place to be. Um, I'm trying to do more of that myself. Kareem gave me a really good reminder of that. The third thing is I like his line, devotion versus discipline. It's really hard to scale a startup without real devotion from your employees. And your vision and your story has to be really compelling. And if it's not, you should work on that. You yourself need to be really compelling. You need to inspire followership. You want people to want to kind of walk across broken glass to work for you. And like your company probably has stuff hanging on the walls, you know, slogans and things you come up with—your culture code stuff. It's incredibly important that you don't just talk to talk, but actually walk the walk on those slogans on the wall. I'll leave you those three. Hope you liked it. I really enjoyed him. See you next time.
turns.zh: 嘿，各位，希望你们喜欢这期和 Kareem 的节目。我真的很享受这次对话。我有很多收获。我给你们讲其中三点，再讲几个我自己的相关故事。呃，两天前我和 Kareem、高盛的 David Solomon 以及 Kshi 的 CEO TK 一起吃了顿饭。我晚餐最大的感受是：“天哪，这三个智人差别也太大了，而且他们的 CEO 打法也完全不同。”这让我想起一句老话，我觉得是：“做你自己，其他人已经有人做了。”我想是王尔德说的。我把这句话留给你们。希望你们能做自己，因为其他人已经有人做了。做 CEO 有很多种方式。我总在找那唯一的方式。事实是做 CEO 成功的路径有很多。嗯，第二点是，他有点像哲学家——他让我想起了一些我一直在思考的东西。人们说，活在过去的人倾向于抑郁，活在未来的人倾向于焦虑，活在当下的人会稍微快乐一点。我自己倾向于活在未来，所以有点焦虑。我记得我焦虑最严重的时候——这可能也正发生在你身上，所以我分享一下。我记得有一次开全员会，大概 100 到 150 名员工，我看着台下，心想：天哪，有这么多人依赖我做出正确的决策。他们要养孩子，要还房贷，很多时候还要照顾父母。实际上我焦虑的增长不是在最初艰难的时候，而是当我们真的在 Scaling（规模扩张）、开始做得很好的时候。总之，如果你也是这样，那就提醒一下自己：活在当下是一个好的状态。嗯，我也在努力这么做。Kareem 真的提醒了我这一点。第三点是，我喜欢他说的“奉献 vs 纪律”。如果没有员工真正的奉献，你很难 Scaling（规模扩张）一家创业公司。你的愿景和故事必须非常有说服力。如果没有，你应该去打磨它。你自己本身也要非常有说服力。你需要激发别人追随你。你要让人愿意为你踩着碎玻璃走过来。还有，你的公司墙上可能挂着一些东西，你知道的，那些口号、你想出来的东西、你的文化准则之类。极其重要的是，你不能只是说说而已，而是要真正做到那些墙上的口号。我就跟你们分享这三点。希望你们喜欢。我真的很喜欢他。下次见。

tldr.en: Wholeness, not lack, drives sustainable success; presence prevents future-obsessed damage.
tldr.zh: 完整而非匮乏驱动可持续的成功；活在当下可避免执迷未来造成的伤害。

tldr.en: Chasing the biggest opportunity delayed Clay; narrowing focus accelerated progress.
tldr.zh: 追逐最大机会让 Clay 停滞；收窄焦点才加速了进展。

tldr.en: Radical transparency and power over simplicity are unexpected levers for trust and product.
tldr.zh: 彻底透明与“强大优先于简单”是建立信任与产品的意外杠杆。

qs.zh: 如何基于完整而非匮乏来打造公司？

qs.en: Why does narrowing focus beat chasing the biggest opportunity?
qs.zh: 为什么收窄焦点胜过追逐最大机会？

qs.en: How does radical transparency create trust with customers?
qs.zh: 彻底透明如何与客户建立信任？
